title: What Nikole Hannah-Jones Wouldn’t Let Herself See
author: Jennifer Weber
summary: Manhattan Institute fellow Jennifer Weber argues that Nikole Hannah-Jones's own reporting shows her daughter was failed not by segregation but by failed pedagogy and equity policies that eroded standards. She walks through the evidence: a teacher who did not assess Najya's reading until pressed, a math folder of ungraded and mostly wrong work, and A's in eighth-grade algebra followed by a failed Regents exam. Weber contrasts this with half a century of evidence, including Project Follow Through, favoring direct instruction with frequent checking and correction over discovery models. She connects Najya's path to de Blasio-era changes such as eliminating school letter grades and replacing test-based promotion with principal-reviewed portfolios, and cites research that fifth-grade understanding of fractions and division best predicts later algebra. She also rebuts the underfunding claim with P.S. 307's per-pupil spending, concluding that those classrooms would have failed any child.
points: Weber argues Najya's teacher assessed her reading only after Hannah-Jones questioned the results.
Project Follow Through found direct instruction outperformed discovery models for disadvantaged children.
New York replaced test-based promotion decisions with principal-reviewed portfolios in 2014, allowing unchecked advancement.
A 2012 study found fifth-grade knowledge of fractions and division predicts high school algebra better than IQ or family income.
The SHSAT and algebra Regents gave a more accurate picture of Najya's knowledge than her transcript.
quotes: How does a child with two educated, affluent, involved parents, in the highest-spending school system in the country, reach ninth grade without knowing fractions? Hannah-Jones’s own reporting shows how: through failed pedagogy.
Decades of research on ongoing assessment have shown that teachers who measure regularly and adjust their instruction get better results than those who don’t.
The discovery models, however, had a built-in appeal for many educators: they made it acceptable not to provide feedback or assess students.
And that’s precisely what Najya didn’t get—the feedback. She thought her answers were correct. Every answer not checked was, in the end, tallied in her favor.
Thereafter, a child could go from one grade to the next, as Najya did, without anyone checking that she had actually learned what she was supposed to learn in the previous grade.

A 2012 study, tracking thousands of students in the United States and the United Kingdom, found that a fifth-grader’s understanding of fractions and division better predicts achievement in high school algebra than anything else, including IQ and family income.
Hannah-Jones concludes that segregation failed her daughter. But those P.S. 307 classrooms would have failed any child, regardless of color.
